items.title: The Guardian view on noise pollution: keep it down | Editorial
items.blurb:
New research linking the issue to Parkinson’s disease adds to the evidence of serious health repercussions from traffic volume and other sources

The roar of late-night traffic is not just annoying for those trying to sleep. It can also have profound effects on their health. A pioneering new study, published this month, has found a clear link between road noise and Parkinson’s disease. The research, which followed more than 3 million Danish participants, found a modest but consistent effect: for every 11.5dB rise in noise level, the risk of the degenerative disorder rose by 3% over the 18-year study.

The study adds to the growing body of evidence that auditory nuisance is associated with serious physical consequences. The European Environment Agency reported last year that more than 110 million people across the continent suffer high levels of health-damaging noise pollution, with physiological stress and sleep disturbance leading to 66,000 early deaths annually as well as heart disease, diabetes and depression. It found that the harm caused was greater than from secondhand tobacco smoke exposure.

items.blurb:
Some have called for Nuremberg-style trials against big oil. But there are laws already on the books to describe companies’ conduct

The sky outside is hazy orange, and my five-year-old son is screaming bloody murder. “Sorry, buddy, we have to stay inside,” I say. “It’s not safe to breathe out there.” I had told him we’d be going to the beach today. Something inside me tears a little as I wonder how many promises he’ll see similarly broken in the coming years.

Far too many parents were forced to have some version of this conversation with their children this month, as smoke from record-breaking wildfires poured across the midwest and north-east. Some of them already had to tell their kids that their Fourth of July festivities were canceled because of the lethal heatwave that caused numerous mass casualty events earlier this month.

The houses in his village are built from stone and mud, which makes them extremely vulnerable to heavy rains. After days of rain, Gul’s kitchen collapsed and his neighbour, Sayed Afsar Sadat, saw a large part of his house completely destroyed. “Rains like this are coming heavier and earlier each year,” says Sadat. “They are destroying the roads and washing away our crops. items.title: 'Trump Needs a Way Out of This War': General Yakovlev explains 'charade' over US-Iran negotiations
items.blurb: Eve Irvine is pleased to welcome General Michel Yakovleff, Professor at Sciences-Po and Former Vice-Chief of Staff at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (Shape).. He presents a strategic rather than tactical reading of the current lull in the US-Iran conflict. He argues that the apparent de-escalation is not evidence of diplomatic progress but of mounting structural constraints. Rather than viewing pauses in hostilities as signs of imminent peace, he frames them as consequences of political pressure, military logistics and industrial limitations. At the centre of his argument is the proposition that modern warfare is ultimately governed by sustainability. Missile stockpiles, industrial production capacity, domestic political legitimacy and alliance commitments become as decisive as battlefield success. General Yakovleff contends that the United States retains ample military capability to continue operations against Iran in isolation, yet doing so progressively erodes its ability to deter other adversaries, reassure allies and sustain global commitments.

items.title: Spies in the sky: how worried should we be about the arrival of AI-enabled smart lamp-posts?
items.blurb:
The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?

How would you feel if your neighbourhood lamp-posts could recognise your number plate, and also your face? Maybe you wouldn’t mind, given how long we’ve had automatic number plate recognition and CCTV. What about if that lamp-post could power itself through its own solar panels, and perhaps find another use for any extra power generated – that would be good, right? This is what Conflow Power Group (CPG) in Warwickshire claims for its iLamps, the first of their kind in the UK.

What if lamp-posts had the potential to incorporate new AI capability – gait analysis, suspicious behaviours – that you haven’t even heard of? This is what the organisation Big Brother Watch worries about. And what if the home secretary had explicitly said she believed in a “panopticon state” – that is, a state that could watch you at all times (as Shabana Mahmood already has) – and what if she still had a job when the lamp-post eyes got their updates? Or what if the next home secretary was even keener on hyper-surveillance (hard to imagine), and the street apparatus was already in place? What about all the data this would harvest – who would own it?

Pete Goding has been photographing the Tour de France for 20 years – here he gives an insight into what it’s been like to document this year’s race

Twenty Tours de France. It seems faintly ridiculous when I write it down. My first was the year Lance Armstrong’s carefully constructed empire was beginning to wobble. I photographed him circling the Champs-Élysées with a film SLR, blissfully unaware that neither film cameras nor Armstrong’s reputation would age particularly well.

Today I’m back where it all began, sitting outside a cafe a stone’s throw from Place de la Concorde nursing a café crème while Paris carries on entirely oblivious. A couple laugh over breakfast. Someone walks an exceptionally pampered poodle. A waiter in a waistcoat unsuccessfully attempts to persuade two tourists that vodka is an acceptable accompaniment to a croissant. In a few hours the world’s biggest bike race will thunder through these streets. Right now, it’s just another Sunday morning.

items.title: A School Computer Changed His Life, Now He Helps 300 Children Get the Same Chance
items.blurb: At 11, Vivek Shangari found the thing that would one day give him back his life. It was 1987. He was walking down a school corridor in Bhilai, Chhattisgarh, when he looked through a doorway and saw four BBC Micros being set up by technicians. On one screen, a ping pong game was running. There were no computer teachers then. No curriculum. No one to guide him. There was only a thick manual and BBC Basic, the programming language that appeared every time the machine was switched on. So, while his classmates went outside to play cricket during lunch breaks, Vivek went to the computer lab. Every lunch break. Every library period. Every games period. When school hours were not enough, he found another way. In Bhilai, some enterprising citizens had begun renting out computers by the hour for Rs 10. Vivek had a piggy bank, given to him by his grandmother to teach him the value of saving. He used those savings to teach himself computers. Years later, the same self-taught skill would help him survive homelessness, build companies, and create wealth. Today, Vivek has donated more than 96 percent of his wealth to a trust that supports children who cannot afford education. “I will not romanticise what came next. Being homeless at 18 is not an adventure. It is cold and exhausting and profoundly lonely,” says Vivek, now 49. His story is also the story of LivingMyPromise, a community of Indians who believe that philanthropy can begin much before one becomes a billionaire. Those who join the community must be over 18 years of age and have a net worth of Rs 1 crore. They pledge 50 percent of their wealth to charitable causes of their choice, either during their lifetime or in their will. LivingMyPromise members gathered in Delhi for the community’s annual meeting in 2023. The pledge is moral and personal. It is made over email. There is no legal document binding the person to it. Yet, for the people who make this promise, it becomes a way of thinking about security, family, legacy, and what it means to have enough. A school lab, a manual, and a boy who taught himself Vivek was four years old when he lost his mother. His father, who struggled with alcoholism and gambling, could not take care of him and his little sister. The children were handed over to their uncle, who took charge unwillingly. Vivek was poor at studies. When he was in his first year of college, his uncle stopped funding his education. Worse, he threw him out of the house. By then, Vivek had one thing he could trust: his ability to programme. He approached the owner of a computer institute in Bhilai and told him about his coding skills. “I told him about my coding skills. He gave me a test and since I did very well, I got a job as a part-time instructor and lab assistant. I was allowed to stay at the institute. I was surrounded by 20 computers and hundreds of books on computer science, maths and physics! I used these to teach myself what I had failed to learn in school,” he says. By the late 1990s, India’s IT revolution was beginning to gather pace. In October 1998, a friend returned from Bengaluru and handed Vivek some books wrapped in a Bengaluru newspaper. His friend thought he was giving him reading material. For Vivek, the newspaper opened a doorway. Inside it was a job advertisement from a company in Bengaluru looking for freshers who could programme in C and C++, the two languages Vivek loved most. He borrowed money, bought a train ticket, travelled to Bengaluru, took the test, and returned to Bhilai to wait. The phone number on his resume was that of the computer training institute where he worked, because he did not own a phone. When the call came, the offer was Rs 7,000 a month. “They noted, gently, that since I had no formal degree, they would start me lower than my peers and observe my performance. I agreed immediately, on the call, and then asked them to book my train ticket. They did,” he recalls. When Vivek arrived in Bengaluru, his boss told him the job involved ANSI Common Lisp and Calculus. It frightened him. His mathematics teacher in school had once declared him a failure in front of the entire class. Now, the job was asking him to do the one thing he believed he could not do. His boss, who was based in the US, became the mentor he had never had. He told Vivek to calm down. He sent books from America. He gave him time, patience, and the rare gift of believing that he was capable of more than he thought. Vivek Shangari has donated over 96 percent of his wealth and supports 300 children. Then something changed. Vivek realised he was good at it. Mathematics, the subject once used as evidence of his inadequacy, became something he genuinely loved. “That was my first real awakening. Not the job. Not the salary. The discovery that I was not the student who had failed. I was the student who had never been properly taught,” he says. Vivek became so absorbed in learning that he began teaching others. First, he taught colleagues on weekends. Then freshers. Then the security guard’s children, the office help’s children, and anyone in the neighbourhood who wanted to learn. “My company gave me the resources. I gave everything I had. And I discovered something that has shaped every decision I have made since: the more you give, the more you receive. Not metaphorically. Literally. In every measurable way,” he says. After one year at Rs 7,000 a month, the company raised his salary to Rs 40,000. In the year 2000, in Bengaluru, as a single person, that was a fortune. Vivek spent four years at ICS. He then worked with Andale and ICICI oneSource. In 2006, he started AceNgage, which had a management buyout in 2010 after it turned profitable. That same year, he started two more things: Vichaar Foundation, and a company called codeCraft. The Common Lisp that had once intimidated him became central to codeCraft’s work. The company was building adaptive AI query resolution in ANSI Common Lisp at a time when artificial intelligence had yet to become a buzzword. Then a Fortune 100 company entered India through its subsidiary. Its flagship search engine, A9, was written almost entirely in Lisp. The company needed Lisp engineers. As it happened, codeCraft had the largest concentration of Lisp engineers in Bengaluru. They made an offer. It was an acquihire. Vivek had taught himself BBC Basic in a school corridor in Bhilai in 1987 because there was no one else to teach him. Twenty-six years later, a Fortune 100 company bought his firm because of that obsession and his refusal to stop learning. From homelessness to helping 300 children study Vivek built companies and made money. Then, he made a decision that confused many people around him. He gave almost all of it away. “I have a home of my own. I have medical insurance. I am well-to-do for a single person. What more do I need?” asks Vivek with a gentle smile. The decision came from a place he had carried since he was 18. “When I was in a dire situation as a youngster, the universe took care of me. I decided when the right time came and I had resources of my own, I would give back more than I had received,” he says. Vivek secured enough investments to generate passive income for his own sustenance and built an emergency fund. Everything else, including his salary from Ace Hacker, goes into a trust called Eklavya, which he started with two friends. He does not draw a salary anymore. He lives on the returns from his investments. Eklavya does one thing: it finds children who cannot afford education and pays for their needs. Fees. Resources. Support. The work Vivek is proudest of happens in rural areas, where the trust meets parents whose children are working instead of studying. The team makes them an offer: let the child go to school full-time, let them study and play and simply be a child, and the trust will take care of every expense. LivingMyPromise members visited Gadchiroli in 2023 as part of the community’s field engagement. The only condition is that the child must never return to work. “Education is not a part-time arrangement. Childhood is not negotiable,” says Vivek. The first year, he says, moved slowly because they were building the infrastructure, fraud detection systems, and processes to ensure the money reached the child. They sponsored a handful of children while setting up those systems. In the two years since, Eklavya has sponsored 300 children. The trust spends between Rs 80,000 and Rs 1 lakh per child per year. So far, it has invested Rs 2.5 crore in 300 futures. Vivek, who still does not have a college degree, believes no child should be deprived of education because of lack of financial support. This belief also brought him to LivingMyPromise. How a group of volunteers turned giving into a pledge LivingMyPromise, or LMP, was modelled on The Giving Pledge, a global initiative through which billionaires commit to giving away a large part of their wealth. LMP takes a similar idea and brings it to Indians who have achieved a degree of financial security. The initiative was launched in 2018 with six members. Four of them were Daan Utsav volunteers: Girish Batra, who first had the idea for LMP, Rama Arya, Bharati Dasgupta, and Venkat Krishnan. The other two founding members were Amit Chandra and Sridhar Rajagopalan, who support Daan Utsav but are not active volunteers. LivingMyPromise began in 2018 with six founding promisors and a 50 percent wealth pledge. Daan Utsav grew out of the Joy of Giving Week, a national celebration of giving that began in 2009. Girish had volunteered for the Joy of Giving Week that year, where he connected with Venkat Krishnan, one of the founders of GiveIndia. For Girish, giving was something he had grown up around. “We were spiritually inclined as a family, so giving was natural. We never felt insecure about the future. I come from a middle-class family. Shopping for clothes was a luxury. We went for two holidays in the first 20 years of my life. But we were content. Our lifestyle was minimalist. My father gave us a good education. His mantra was: hard work leads to money. I was lucky to be good at studies and completed engineering and MBA courses. After several years in the corporate sector, I now support startups,” Girish shares. His own understanding of wealth changed as he built his career. “I support the act of wealth creation. But I believe that the best use of wealth is giving back to society. Beyond a point, getting a bigger home or bigger car gives no satisfaction. With this belief in mind, we decided to pledge 50 percent of our wealth to charitable causes. My wife Tanu, who is a yoga teacher, is also a promisor,” says Girish. Girish Batra and his wife Tanu pledged 50 percent of their wealth through LivingMyPromise. The Giving Pledge had around 200 promisors at the time, including four Indians such as Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw and Azim Premji. “When you speak to people, you realise that folks from all segments of society are happy to give. I have heard stories of vegetable vendors and auto drivers who have given to help others. That’s because there is a joy in giving,” he relates. Gunjan Thaney has led LivingMyPromise for five years and is currently based in Australia. Gunjan Thaney, who now heads LMP, says the premise was simple: if billionaires could make such a public pledge, Indians with financial security could also think deeply about how much they truly need and how much they can give. From six founding promisors in 2018, the community has grown to 175 promisors, including individuals and couples. The Rs 1 crore question behind the pledge To join LMP, a person must be over 18 years of age and have a net worth of at least Rs 1 crore. The threshold is an eligibility criterion. LMP says it is meant for people who have achieved financial security, including salaried professionals, government employees, small business owners, and first-generation entrepreneurs who have built wealth gradually through savings, home ownership, and long-term investments. In the Indian context, LMP says, many people with a net worth of Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore fall into this category. An average 2BHK in Mumbai or Delhi alone costs over Rs 1 crore, the team points out. Someone who has not reached this level of wealth is unlikely to be able to give away half their wealth without putting their own security at risk. “There is no right time or age to take the pledge. You have to be over 18 years of age and have a net worth of Rs 1 crore, including property. Our youngest promisor is 27 while our oldest is 80 years old. We have couples where only one member is a promisor. We have single women who don’t have children as promisors. The pledge can be taken by Indians living anywhere in the world,” explains Gunjan, who has been running the initiative for five years. The net worth includes all assets that belong entirely to the person, including the home they live in, inheritance, property, jewellery, investments, and assets in India or anywhere else, after subtracting liabilities. A spouse’s assets are included only when the couple signs up together. LMP does not independently verify a person’s net worth before they join. The pledge is based on trust and individual integrity. Prospective promisors are usually introduced through existing members or trusted networks. If someone reaches LMP through the website, Gunjan has a detailed conversation with them to understand their lifestyle, needs, family situation, and philanthropic intent. “Our community is still small. New promisors are mostly known to existing ones. If someone new reaches us through our website, I have a detailed discussion with them to get a sense of their lifestyle, needs and family. We encourage the promisor to discuss with his spouse and children before taking the pledge. They have to be on the same page. Once I am convinced about their intentions, I have an existing promisor talk to them. Then we invite the person to join the community,” says Gunjan. Although there is no legal binding, LMP insists that each promisor’s name is listed publicly on its website. “While there is no legal binding to the LMP pledge, we insist that the promisor’s name is listed on our website. Almost 99 percent of our promisors want to remain anonymous, but we do not give them that option. The purpose of making their names public is to inspire others to follow suit. The only way to join this community is to be open about it,” says Gunjan. A promisor’s name, photograph, and statement of purpose are published on the LMP website. Other personal details, including contact information, net worth, asset details, and current or future giving plans, are kept confidential. Why education leads the giving list For many promisors, the pledge is only the beginning. The harder question is where and how to give. Susai Anthony, 30, is the giving manager at LMP and has been with the initiative for two years. He has a graduate and postgraduate degree in social work. “The most common age group of promisors is the 55 to 80 age group. Among the total promisors, around 30 percent are couples. Among the individual promisors, 70 percent are men and 30 percent are women,” he says. Susai Anthony helps promisors identify causes and understand possible avenues for giving The promisor community comes from different professional backgrounds. Corporate sector professionals make up 32.7 percent, social sector professionals 26.5 percent, entrepreneurs 14.3 percent, retired professionals 9.8 percent, professionals such as doctors, artists and writers 5.8 percent, freelancers 5.4 percent, homemakers 4.5 percent, and those from family business backgrounds 1 percent. Women promisors are part of a community that has grown from six members to 175 since 2018. The five causes closest to LMP donors are education, livelihood and skills development, health and medical relief, disability inclusion, and rural and tribal development. Education receives the highest level of interest and support. This includes primary, secondary and higher education, vocational training, technical education, research, scholarships, informal education, and related initiatives. Around 30 to 40 percent of promisors plan to give through their will. The rest, like Vivek, give during their lifetime. Susai helps promisors identify a cause. Once they choose an area, such as elderly care, he researches the subject and maps different possibilities for donation. He also helps them with the process of giving. The LMP team identifies non-profit organisations through social incubators, trusted networks, and other credible sources. They have initial conversations with these organisations, assess their work, and share insights with the relevant promisors. The final decision rests with the promisor. Each promisor engages directly with the organisation and decides whether to support it. LMP does not conduct formal due diligence for promisors. It also does not track or monitor later interactions, funding decisions, or the impact of donations. These remain private and are managed independently by each promisor. Many promisors voluntarily share their annual giving details with LMP. So far, more than 100 of the 175 promisors have done so. The initiative maintains a broad understanding of each promisor’s giving plans, interests, and commitments, while respecting their privacy. LivingMyPromise members met in Goa in 2024 to exchange experiences around planned giving. At present, all signatories are part of a closely connected community, where each member is personally known to at least one other member. As the community grows, LMP hopes to preserve these trusted relationships through regular engagement. The team also connects promisors who support similar cause areas, so they can learn from each other, share experiences, and collaborate where useful. The family conversations behind giving away wealth A pledge to give away half of one’s wealth naturally affects family conversations, especially with children. The LMP team has spoken to children of parents who have become promisors. Gunjan says many of them respond with warmth and maturity. A common view is: give us a good education, and then do whatever you want with your wealth. Many children, she says, appreciate their parents for donating to social causes. For Dev Sinha, 20, the son of promisor couple Dhiraj Sinha and Deepali Bhagat, the conversation began when he was 15. Dev is now studying BBA in Bengaluru. His father has spent many years in the corporate sector, while his mother is a distributor for edtech products. “One day, my father came up to me and asked me if I was okay if he donated 50 percent of his wealth to social causes. I told him I had no problem. I felt I was living a privileged life and if some of my parents’ wealth could help underprivileged people, it would be great,” says Dev. Dev Sinha supported his parents’ decision to pledge half their wealth when he was 15 years old. His parents have donated to education, healthcare and disability inclusion. They have also contributed their time, skills and experience. “My parents have always been socially conscious and taking the pledge has been an opportunity for them to support the causes they care about, and give back to society. The causes they have donated to so far are education, healthcare and disability inclusion. They have not just donated money. They also contributed their time, skills and experience. This has been an important influence on me. It has reshaped my thinking on responsibility and giving back,” says Dev. Why LMP asks for such a big commitment For LMP, the 50 percent pledge is intentional. Gunjan says the number is meant to attract people who have thought deeply about how much they need and how much they can give. “We do not take anything from anybody. There is no incentive to join LMP. The most expensive thing you can commit to is half your wealth. We want the right people to join us. Those who are willing to do this. We don’t want to make the community bigger by offering lower levels of donation,” she explains. Promisors can change their mind and back out, especially in the event of an unforeseen need such as a major health requirement. Gunjan says many members plan carefully before making the pledge. “Most promisors have budgeted for major expenses. Most have taken health insurance. They have budgeted for children’s education and a home for themselves. So, they are not worried about the future and can actively focus on giving. Still, if they want to back out, they can. There is nothing binding them legally,” she explains. Tax benefits are not linked to joining LMP. Each country has its own rules, and tax benefits apply only when promisors donate to an eligible organisation. LMP itself is a fully community-managed initiative. Its operating expenses, including salaries for the core team, are funded through contributions pooled by the promisors. Currently, the three core team members are employed through the payroll of two organisations operated by two of the promisors. “We conduct events and meets where everyone pays for their own travel and stay,” says Gunjan. What they hope to build by 2030 Gunjan, who is now based in Australia, spent a decade in the wealth management space, helping high net-worth individuals make more money. She wanted to do something more meaningful. Life came full circle. She now helps people give away their wealth. For LMP, giving is a personal choice, but it is also a cultural act. The public pledge is meant to inspire more people to think about wealth, legacy, and responsibility. The initiative does not do fundraising. It serves as a platform where people can connect, learn, share ideas, and give more meaningfully. LivingMyPromise’s 2026 annual meeting in Mumbai brought members of the promisor community together. LMP aims to expand its community to 500 members by 2030. For Vivek, the idea remains deeply personal. Long before he had money to give, people gave him chances: access to a computer lab, a place to sleep, books from a mentor, and faith at a moment when he had none in himself. Now, through Eklavya and LivingMyPromise, he is passing that forward to children whose futures can change with the same simple gift he once received: the chance to learn.

items.title: How Drones Helped Rescue Teams Reach Flood-Hit Families in Gujarat
items.blurb: The latest spell of monsoon rain has brought more than just heavy showers to Gujarat. Floodwaters have submerged homes, disrupted livelihoods and left hundreds of people stranded as rescue teams race against time to reach those trapped. Across several affected areas, familiar roads disappeared beneath muddy currents. Entire neighbourhoods were cut off, leaving families stranded on rooftops, inside schools and in waterlogged homes. For many, rescue was no longer a matter of distance but of access. While the Army, local authorities and emergency responders worked tirelessly to evacuate people, another kind of support was taking shape in the skies. In Dholka, drones helped rescuers locate stranded residents, assess flooded areas and deliver essential supplies to places that had become nearly impossible to reach. A startup steps into the rescue effort Among the organisations supporting the operation was Prime UAV, a drone technology company based in Mehsana, Gujarat. Founded in 2019 by Pradip Patel and Hiten Patel, the startup develops unmanned aerial solutions for agriculture, infrastructure inspections, mapping, surveying and disaster response. It is also recognised by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT). Founders Pradip Patel and Hiten Patel helped strengthen flood response efforts through drone-based aerial surveillance. Photograph: (Prime UAV) Over the years, the company has expanded beyond commercial drone services to build expertise in aerial surveillance, mapping and customised drone solutions — capabilities that become especially valuable during natural disasters, when speed, visibility and access can make a critical difference. This was not the company's first emergency deployment. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Prime UAV supported local authorities with sanitisation efforts and lockdown monitoring. In 2020, it also deployed drones during the locust invasion that affected crops across Gujarat and Rajasthan. According to CEO Pradip Patel, those experiences shaped the team's disaster-response approach and reinforced the role drones can play during public emergencies. Reaching places rescuers couldn't When reports emerged that people were stranded in Dholka, the Prime UAV team immediately mobilised and joined local authorities and relief personnel. "When we learned that children and residents were stranded due to severe flooding in the Dholka region, we felt an immediate responsibility to act. We strongly believe that technology should serve society during times of crisis," tells Patel to The Better India. "Within 30 minutes of receiving the information, our emergency response team, along with rescue and surveillance drones, was mobilised and dispatched to the affected area." Emergency responders and local authorities work to evacuate flood-affected families while drone-based aerial monitoring strengthens situational awareness during critical rescue efforts. Photograph: (Prime UAV) In several locations, rescue teams first used tractors and boats to reach flood-hit areas before drones surveyed the terrain from above. The drones provided real-time aerial views of inundated neighbourhoods, helping responders identify stranded people and assess the scale of flooding. Their role became even more valuable after sunset, when poor visibility made ground operations increasingly difficult. According to the company, the drones continued monitoring flooded areas through the night, giving rescue teams a clearer picture of conditions on the ground . Patel says features such as GPS-enabled location tracking, live aerial feeds and payload delivery systems proved especially useful during the operation. The live footage helped responders identify priority locations and plan safer routes through floodwaters. Meanwhile, customised payload systems enabled essential supplies to reach places inaccessible by road or boat. Although Prime UAV did not carry out evacuations directly, its drones strengthened ongoing rescue operations by helping teams locate stranded residents, assess inaccessible areas and make faster decisions. "The mission demonstrated how drones can significantly improve situational awareness and response efficiency during disasters," Patel says. Technology supporting people At its heart, this story is not about drones. It is about families waiting to be rescued, children sheltering in schools, emergency workers navigating dangerous conditions and communities coming together during a crisis. Technology simply gave those responders another tool. Flood-hit neighbourhoods in Dholka remained inaccessible by road and boat in several locations, prompting the use of drones to map affected areas and deliver crucial information to rescue teams. Photograph: ( Navjeevan Express ) Drones cannot replace rescue workers, but they can help them locate stranded people more quickly, assess risks in real time and deliver supplies to areas that remain cut off. The collaboration between emergency responders and technology providers in Dholka shows how innovation can strengthen traditional rescue efforts rather than replace them. A new chapter in disaster response As extreme weather events become more frequent and monsoon floods continue to affect communities across India, technology is becoming an increasingly important part of disaster management. The Gujarat flood response showed how technology and human effort can work together, with drones helping rescuers reach stranded communities when every minute mattered. Photograph: ( The Hawk ) In Gujarat, amid rising floodwaters and widespread disruption, Prime UAV's intervention offered a glimpse of how locally developed technology can support emergency responders when every minute counts. The real story is not the drones themselves, but the people they helped rescuers reach — a reminder that innovation, when used for the public good, can become a lifeline in times of crisis. Sources: Prime UAV 'Gujarat floods: Drone startup helps in Dholka rescue operations' by Press Trust Of India. items.title: This Delhi Mom Beat Burnout By Growing Tiny Green Paradise In Her 98 Sq Ft Balcony
items.blurb: The clock had just touched 11 on a weekday morning when I called Dipalee Nitin Rahangdale. On the other side of the phone came the soft sound of water splashing against terracotta pots, followed by a warm voice asking me to wait for a moment. “I am just watering my plants. Can you give me a minute?” she asks gently. A few moments later, the rustling leaves settled into the background as she returned to the call from the balcony of her rented apartment in Delhi. At 32, she speaks with a calmness that comes from finding inner peace after emotionally exhausting years, and from learning to rebuild life slowly through nature and creative expression . Her balcony is not grand by any means. Measuring just 14 by 7 feet, it is small, compact, and tucked into a city apartment. Within this limited space, she has created something astonishing. Hanging vines spill gracefully from railings, philodendrons curl around shelves, money plants trail across corners, and nearly 50 plants stand healthy under her care. Every inch of the balcony carries intention, patience, and healing, making it feel alive beyond its greenery alone. "Gardening became therapy for me," she says softly. "People think peace comes from money, success, or other people. But emotionally, everyone needs something that belongs only to them. You need a hobby that heals you from within. For me, that became gardening." Today, thousands of people know her through her Instagram page, @WabiSabiWithDipalee , where she shares glimpses of slow living, indoor gardening, and mindful spaces. Her videos are comforting and easy to follow. There are no extravagant makeovers or luxury aesthetics designed purely for social media validation. Instead, her content reflects ordinary life in a simple, beautiful way. A woman watering plants in the morning sunlight. A mother preparing potting mix with her child. Peaceful reflections about mental health, patience, and finding beauty in imperfection. It is this honesty that has helped her build a loyal online community of over 4,069 followers who connect with the peaceful world she has created. Her journey feels even more touching because this little balcony garden has become a shared space between her and her six-year-old son, Kavish. While many parents struggle to pull children away from screens, he spends his afternoons helping his mother water plants, plant seeds, and rearrange pots. Sometimes, he leaves cartoons midway to sit beside her while she works with soil and leaves. Together, mother and son are growing something bigger than a garden. The corporate life that slowly drained her Before becoming a gardening content creator, Dipalee spent years working in the corporate sector while trying to balance marriage, motherhood, and constant work schedules. Like many women, she strongly valued financial independence and wanted to build her own identity through work. Every inch of the balcony carries intention, patience, and healing, making it feel alive beyond its greenery alone. "I always wanted my own identity and the ability to stand on my own feet, so being financially independent and earning for myself was always something that mattered to me," she says in a conversation with The Better India . But slowly, the pressure of corporate life began draining her emotionally. Her office hours officially stretched from 9.30 in the morning to 7 in the evening, but reality was far harsher. Meetings continued late into the night because senior management arrived towards the end of the day. By the time she returned home, it was nearly 9 pm, and whatever energy remained had already been consumed by exhaustion. "I could not spend time with my son," she recalls. "The whole day would disappear in work, and I used to come home feeling emotionally empty." In June 2023, after years of pushing herself through exhaustion, she made the difficult decision to quit her job, one that felt especially hard for someone who valued independence and self-identity . "Leaving work affects you mentally, especially as a woman, when there is a sense of guilt attached to stepping away from a career, but I came to realise that I needed peace, and I needed time for myself and my child," she says. Her elder sister, Rupali Ravindra Rahangdale, watched this emotional transition closely from Pune. According to her, the difference between the Dipalee of a few years ago and the woman she is today is impossible to ignore. "She was constantly stressed because of work," she says. "I had seen her become mentally exhausted. But gardening changed her completely. It made her calmer, more positive, and much more patient." Throughout her difficult phases, Rupali became one of her strongest emotional support systems. "Whenever she felt demotivated with gardening, I would tell her not to stop and remind her that one day her hard work would pay off, so I shared her videos with people and kept motivating her constantly because I genuinely believed in what she was creating," she says warmly. The childhood memory hidden in marigold flowers Dipalee's connection with plants did not begin in adulthood. It had existed within her since childhood. Growing up in Maharashtra, she was surrounded by homes where gardening was simply a part of life. Her family maintained a kitchen garden like many households around them, but while others focused on vegetables, she found herself naturally drawn towards flowers and decoration. "We used to grow marigold flowers during Diwali," she says with a smile that instantly softens her voice. "I still remember decorating the house with those flowers. Those are some of my happiest childhood memories." Even as a child, she loved arranging spaces and decorating corners beautifully. While many children developed an interest in cooking or household work, she found joy in aesthetics and greenery. "I was never really drawn to cooking," she laughs, "but I have always loved flowers, home decor, and the process of turning spaces into something peaceful." As life became busier, however, gardening slowly disappeared into the background. After moving to Delhi and entering professional life, she barely had time for hobbies. The pace of adulthood consumed her attention completely. Yet somewhere within her, that childhood love for plants remained alive. Her journey feels even more touching because this little balcony garden has become a shared space between her and her six-year-old son, Kavish. Then came August 2019, a turning point she now looks back on with gratitude. After switching jobs and spending more time at home, she bought her very first plants . "I started with a money plant, aloe vera, and tulsi, just very easy-to-care-for plants that could survive without much effort," she recalls. At the time, she had no idea those three plants would eventually transform her entire life. The plants that died before the garden bloomed Like many beginners, she initially learnt gardening through YouTube videos and internet tutorials. But the process came with confusion, mistakes, and heartbreak. "A lot of my plants died in the beginning," she says honestly. "Sometimes because of wrong information online, and sometimes because I did not understand the plant properly." One of her biggest lessons came through jade plants. "Everyone used to say jade plants are indoor plants, even nursery owners would sell them that way, but when I observed them closely myself, I realised they actually need bright sunlight to survive," she explains. At another point, she followed online advice suggesting kitchen waste could be directly added into soil as fertiliser, but she later realised that only peels were actually helpful, while the rest led to fungus and pest attacks that damaged several plants. "I felt terrible," she admits. "There were times when I would almost cry after losing a plant." But slowly, gardening began to teach her lessons that went far beyond plant care, building her into someone more patient, observant, and emotionally strong, even in difficult moments. "Gardening taught me that every environment is different," she explains. "You cannot blindly follow someone else's advice. You need to understand your own home, your sunlight, your balcony, your weather." Over time, her tiny balcony grew into a flourishing indoor foliage garden filled with snake plants, spider plants, philodendrons, money plants, aloe vera, bougainvillea, jade plants, wandering jew plants, umbrella trees, adeniums, lilies, air plants, areca palms, tulsi, zig-zag cactus, and many more varieties. Because the balcony receives limited sunlight, she primarily focuses on foliage plants and low-maintenance greenery. Living in a rented apartment also influenced her gardening style significantly. "I did not have the option of a terrace garden, and moving heavy outdoor plants from one room to another is extremely difficult, especially with monkeys and birds outside that damage them, so indoor gardening became the best solution for me," she explains. Why did she name her page 'Wabi Sabi'? Her Instagram page name, @WabiSabiWithDipalee , reflects the philosophy she now follows consciously. Inspired by the Japanese concept of Wabi Sabi (finding beauty in imperfection), she believes beauty exists in imperfection, simplicity, and authenticity rather than polished perfection. "Social media makes people feel that everything has to look perfect, from homes to aesthetics to lives, but I believe real beauty actually exists in imperfect things too," she says. This philosophy is evident in the way she decorates her balcony . Instead of expensive decor, she reuses simple items creatively, proving that peaceful spaces do not require luxury. For Dipalee, gardening slowly turned into emotional healing. "When I sit with my plants, my stress disappears," she says calmly. "Gardening slows your mind down." Her routine remains intentionally simple. Every day, she spends around half an hour checking soil moisture, watering plants only when necessary, pruning leaves occasionally, and adding vermicompost whenever required. Instead of chemical pesticides, she uses turmeric to prevent fungal infections naturally. "The biggest mistake people make is overwatering," she explains with a laugh. "Plants usually die from too much care rather than too little." The little boy who leaves cartoons for plants But perhaps the most beautiful development has been the bond gardening created between her and Kavish. When Dipalee first became a mother, many people warned her that raising a child and maintaining plants together would be impossible. Even as a child, she loved arranging spaces and decorating corners beautifully. "People used to say that children would spoil plants and throw soil everywhere, but in my experience, my son and my plants grew together naturally, learning to coexist and care for each other over time," she says. Initially, her son occasionally played with soil while crawling around the balcony. But slowly, he began understanding that plants required care and gentleness. Today, at six years old, he actively participates in almost every gardening activity. "He helps me water plants, make potting mix, plant seeds, and repot plants," she says proudly. She believes gardening has changed him emotionally, too. Earlier, like many children, he spent long hours watching cartoons. Now, whenever she works on the balcony, he leaves the television behind and runs towards her eagerly. "He has become more caring," she says. "If he sees a plant somewhere, he immediately asks if we can bring it home." More importantly, gardening has taught him patience and acceptance. "When you plant seeds, they do not grow overnight, so he is learning to be patient, to wait for things to mature slowly, and to understand that not every plant survives, which is also teaching him that failure is a natural part of life," she explains. Sometimes, his innocent dreams leave her emotional. "He tells me that when he grows up, we will open a seed shop together," she says, laughing softly. Growing slowly, but authentically In April 2025, Dipalee finally decided to share her journey online through Instagram. Unlike creators chasing overnight virality, she focused entirely on authenticity. "My audience is growing slowly, but organically," she says. "I want genuine people connecting with me." Today, her content revolves around indoor gardening, balcony decor, mindful living, and emotional well-being through nature. Her videos capture small, personal moments from daily life: rearranging foliage in the morning sunlight, preparing potting mix with Kavish, or discussing mental peace and self-growth. In the future, she hopes to convert her passion into something larger. "I would love to help people create peaceful balcony spaces," she says. "I want to teach them which plants suit different homes and how gardening can improve mental health." And if she ever gets her dream home, she already knows exactly what she wants. "I want either a penthouse or a ground-floor home with lots of gardening space," she says instantly. As our conversation ended, she returned to watering her plants while Kavish hovered nearby excitedly, asking questions about a new sapling they had recently brought home. Watching them together, it became evident that this little balcony was never only about gardening. Every day, she spends around half an hour checking soil moisture, and watering plants only when necessary. It was about healing slowly after burnout. About slowing down in a world obsessed with speed . About finding emotional peace through nature. And perhaps most importantly, it was about understanding that even the smallest rented spaces can bloom beautifully when nurtured with patience and love. All pictures courtesy Dipalee Nitin Rahangdale.

items.title: Unable to Farm After an Accident, 91-YO 'Amma' Grew 3000 Trees Beside Her Kerala Home
items.blurb: For years, Devaki Amma’s days began in the paddy fields of Muthukulam, a coastal village in Kerala’s Alappuzha district. Farming was the rhythm of her life, work she had known since childhood and continued alongside her husband, Gopalakrishna Pillai, a retired headmaster. Then, at 46, a car accident brought that rhythm to a sudden stop. The injury severely restricted her movement, and doctors advised her to avoid physical strain for nearly three years. For someone used to working outdoors from dawn, the long stretch of enforced rest felt unbearable. The fields she had tended for decades were suddenly beyond her reach. Life, as she knew it, had changed overnight. How recovery turned into a habit of planting Confined largely to her home, Devaki Amma began planting a single sapling on the sandy plot near her house, land that had until then only been used for post-harvest activities . It gave her something to do while her body healed. She planted another, then another. There was no plan to build a forest. It was simply a way to pass the days without her usual work. That small, repeated act did not stop once she recovered. Friends and relatives began bringing seeds and cuttings on their visits, and her husband and children joined in the effort. Instead of chemical fertilisers, Devaki Amma relied on leaf litter, mulching and manure from home-reared cattle to steadily improve nutrient-poor coastal sandy soil. Photograph: (AI-Generated image) Her daughter Thankamani, who would go on to head the Environmental Engineering department at a Thiruvananthapuram College, grew up watching this quiet, steady labour. What had started as a way to escape boredom slowly turned into a shared family project, and then into Devaki Amma's life's purpose. Turning sandy land into a living forest Over more than four decades, Devaki Amma's saplings spread across nearly five acres of coastal sandy soil, a stretch of land she named Thapovanam. She worked without formal training, relying instead on close observation of the soil and the local climate . Mulching, organic manure from home-reared cattle, and careful retention of leaf litter gradually improved land that was never expected to hold a forest. As Kerala's monsoon pattern shifted over the decades, with longer dry spells followed by concentrated bursts of heavy rain, Devaki Amma adjusted her methods rather than abandoning them. Her family adapted their mulching techniques at intervals to prevent waterlogging and protect root systems, a set of solutions drawn entirely from years of trial and repeated observation rather than any textbook. Long before receiving the Padma Shri, Devaki Amma's conservation work earned the Indira Priyadarshini Vrikshamitra Award in 2003 and the Nari Shakti Puraskar in 2018. Photograph: ( The Better India ) Two ponds within Thapovanam have never run dry. They support groundwater recharge, help prevent seawater from seeping into the coastal soil, and sustain aquatic life through the year. The forest also holds an Indian bael tree estimated to be around 200 years old, far older than Thapovanam itself, now standing within an ecosystem that grew up around it. 3000 trees in Kerala’s forest-less district Alappuzha is the only district in Kerala without natural forest cover , which makes Thapovanam more remarkable. The forest today holds over 3,000 recorded trees, plants, shrubs and creepers, including rare and medicinal species increasingly hard to find elsewhere in the state. It shelters peacocks, owls, the emerald dove and migratory birds, alongside butterflies and other small wildlife, functioning as a repository for native Kerala plant species under threat from habitat loss. Everything is maintained organically, without chemical fertilisers, using methods Devaki Amma developed over decades of trial and observation. She built all of this without institutional funding or a trained team, working largely without public recognition for most of those four decades. Her methods now draw interest from a newer generation of tree planters, including Krishnakumar S , who has helped build over 40 dense urban forests to cool Indian cities. From one sapling to a Padma Shri Devaki Amma, now 91, is widely known across Kerala as ‘Vanamuthassi’, or grandmother of forests. Her work drew national attention well before this year, including the Indira Priyadarshini Vrikshamitra Award in 2003 and the Nari Shakti Puraskar in 2018, and a mention by former President Ram Nath Kovind in his Republic Day address. This year, she received the Padma Shri, India's fourth-highest civilian honour, in the Unsung Heroes category. and was the only recipient from Kerala. Thapovanam is now visited by students, researchers and nature enthusiasts studying grassroots biodiversity conservation, and Devaki Amma has encouraged schools, colleges and households across the state to grow native and medicinal plants of their own, often providing seeds and seedlings herself. Her daughter Thankamani now cares for her full time, while the rest of the family continues to help maintain the forest. Devaki Amma still tends her plants daily, urging everyone she meets to plant at least one tree. Her four decades of quiet, repeated effort stand as proof of what patience, a family's support and a single sapling can eventually become. Sources: ' Forest Conservationist Devaki Amma Receives Padma Shri from President Droupadi Murmu ': Press Information Bureau, Government of India, Published 2026 ' The grandmother of forests: How Devaki Amma grew a jungle and a legacy ': by Deccan Herald, Published 25 January 2026 ' Padma Shri Awardee Devaki Amma: The Woman Who Grew Forests ': DNN24, Published 31 May 2026

items.title: International Tiger Day: 7 Extraordinary Habitats That Prove Tigers Can Thrive Almost Anywhere
items.blurb: Most of us picture tigers prowling through dense tropical jungles. But the world's largest cat has mastered landscapes far more diverse than popular imagination allows, from icy forests in Russia to tidal mangrove swamps in India, and from towering Himalayan foothills to Southeast Asia's rainforests. On International Tiger Day, here's a journey through the remarkable homes that continue to shelter one of Earth's most iconic predators. A tiger silently padding through waist-high grass. Another weaving through tangled mangrove roots as tides rise around it. Yet another leaving fresh paw prints on snow in temperatures that plunge below -30°C. They all belong to the same species. For centuries, tigers have evolved into masters of adaptation, surviving in landscapes so dramatically different that they seem like homes for entirely different animals. While many people imagine them living exclusively in dense jungles, the tiger's range stretches across some of the planet's most extraordinary ecosystems . These habitats aren't just beautiful — they are among the most biologically rich and ecologically important landscapes on Earth. They also reveal another important fact: saving tigers means protecting an astonishing diversity of ecosystems. 1. The frozen forests of Russia Perhaps the last place anyone expects to find a tiger is in snow. Yet the Amur (Siberian) tiger, the world's largest tiger subspecies, inhabits the coniferous and mixed forests of Russia's Far East, with a small population extending into northeastern China. Winter temperatures here routinely fall below -30°C, and snowfall blankets the forests for months. The Siberian tiger was also called "Amur tiger", "Manchurian tiger", "Korean tiger", and "Ussurian tiger", depending on the region where individuals were observed. Photograph: (Appaloosa/Wikipedia) Unlike their tropical cousins, these tigers have thick fur, larger paws that act like natural snowshoes, and an extra layer of body fat to survive the bitter cold. Their lighter orange coats blend surprisingly well with snowy landscapes broken by tree trunks and winter shadows. It is the northernmost home of any wild tiger on Earth. 2. India's mangrove kingdom Now imagine the exact opposite. Instead of snow, there are shifting tides. Instead of dry forest trails, there are muddy islands crisscrossed by tidal creeks. The Sundarbans, spanning India and Bangladesh, is the world's largest mangrove forest and home to one of the planet's most unique tiger populations. Tigers of world’s largest mangrove forest, Sundarbans Tiger Reserve. pic.twitter.com/ad99AcYKNj — Trikansh Sharma (@trikansh_sharma) April 27, 2026 Here, Bengal tigers have adapted to life among salt-tolerant trees, tidal channels, and muddy terrain. They are exceptional swimmers. As sea levels rise because of climate change, the Sundarbans is also becoming one of the most vulnerable tiger habitats on Earth . 3. The endless grasslands Not all forests are dense. Some tiger landscapes are wide, open grasslands stretching as far as the eye can see. In reserves like Kaziranga, Manas, and Dudhwa, tall elephant grass grows over four metres high, creating natural cover for predators. These floodplain ecosystems are incredibly productive, supporting dense populations of deer, wild pigs, and buffalo, the prey that sustain healthy tiger populations. This tiger was born to sparkle ✨ This Golden Tiger of Kaziranga is worth more than solid gold… VC:In the clip pic.twitter.com/rP0Wc3RRUL — Susanta Nanda IFS (Retd) (@susantananda3) January 30, 2024 The annual floods that replenish these grasslands also maintain one of India's richest wildlife landscapes, shared by rhinos, elephants, swamp deer, and hundreds of bird species. 4. The Himalayan foothills The forests below the Himalayas present yet another world. Protected landscapes such as Corbett, Rajaji, and parts of Bhutan and Nepal combine river valleys, rocky hills, sal forests, and mountain streams. Tigers here navigate steep terrain that demands strength, agility and endurance. Jim Corbett National Park houses a thriving population of over 260 Bengal tigers, boasting one of the highest tiger densities among Indian national parks. Photograph: (Sriroopa Dutta) As temperatures rise globally, scientists believe these higher-elevation forests could become increasingly important for tiger conservation. 5. Southeast Asia's tropical rainforests The rainforests of Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, and Indonesia represent some of the oldest forests on Earth. Dense vegetation, towering trees, and year-round rainfall make them challenging places for both predators and researchers. Tigers living here often have enormous territories because prey densities are lower than in India's grasslands. These forests are biodiversity hotspots, sheltering clouded leopards, sun bears, hornbills, tapirs and countless other species alongside tigers. 6. Dry deciduous forests India's best-known tiger reserves, such as Bandhavgarh, Kanha, Pench, Ranthambore, and Tadoba, lie within dry deciduous forests. Unlike evergreen jungles, these forests change dramatically with the seasons. Leaves fall during summer, creating open woodlands where prey animals become easier to spot. During the monsoon, the forests transform into lush green landscapes teeming with life. A playful cub puts its skills to the test, trying out a stalking trick picked up from its mother. What may look like a game today is actually an important learning phase, helping young tigers understand the wild around them. Every crouch, stalk and surprise. pic.twitter.com/gglIyS9G7K — Pench Tiger Reserve (@PenchMP) June 21, 2026 These habitats support some of the world's highest tiger densities, proving that seasonal forests can be just as important as tropical rainforests. 7. Swamps, wetlands, and riverine forests Many tiger habitats revolve around water. Across India, Nepal and Southeast Asia, riverine forests and wetlands provide year-round prey, dense vegetation and reliable freshwater. These ecosystems also help regulate floods, recharge groundwater, and support millions of people downstream. Protecting tigers here often means safeguarding rivers that sustain both wildlife and human communities. Tiger is an “umbrella species” A tiger is often called an umbrella species, and protecting it means protecting everything beneath that umbrella. Each landscape that shelters tigers also stores carbon, purifies water, supports pollinators and sustains thousands of other plants and animals. The snow forests of Russia regulate northern ecosystems. The Sundarbans buffer devastating cyclones. India's grasslands support endangered rhinos and elephants. Rainforests absorb vast amounts of carbon while harbouring irreplaceable biodiversity. Saving these habitats, therefore, means protecting far more than a single charismatic predator. International Tiger Day is often celebrated with numbers: how many tigers remain, how many reserves exist, how populations have recovered. But perhaps the greatest conservation story lies in the astonishing places it still calls home. The tiger reminds us that resilience is written into nature's most extraordinary landscapes. Protecting the tiger, therefore, is about ensuring that these remarkable worlds, so different from one another, yet equally vital, continue to thrive for generations to come. Sources: ‘Sundarbans may get a bigger tiger reserve: What the proposed habitat merger means for India's mangrove wilderness’ : By First Post Lifestyle Desk, Published on 24 June 2026 ‘Meet the Siberian tiger: The world’s largest cat roaming the Asia's snowy forests’ : by Lindsey Jean Schueman, Published on 4 December 2025 ‘Russia boosts protection for Tigers’ : by Traffic, Published on 30th October 2012

items.title: Why Mumbai Floods and Still Faces Water Shortages
items.blurb: Every monsoon, Mumbai floods. Just a few months later, the same city struggles with water shortages. How can billions of litres of rain fall every year... and still not be enough? 🌧️💧 Singapore once faced a similar challenge. Instead of treating rain as a problem, it redesigned the city to capture, store, and reuse rainwater from rooftops, roads, and drains. The result? Less flooding, greater water security, and a smarter way of living with the climate. As climate change brings more intense rainfall to Indian cities, perhaps the real question isn't how quickly we can drain rainwater away—it's how much of it we can save. Sometimes, the most valuable resource isn't scarce. We're simply letting it slip away. Should Indian cities adopt Singapore's rainwater management model? items.title: One Photographer Got Children to Capture the Side of Chennai's 'Rowdy Area' the World Never Sees
items.blurb: When 20-year-old Rasiya Banu first picked up a DSLR camera, she was terrified. Growing up in Vyasarpadi, a working-class neighbourhood in North Chennai, she had become accustomed to hearing outsiders describe her locality with words like “dangerous”, “dirty”, or “rowdy area”. The labels followed her into classrooms and colleges. They shaped how others saw her before they knew her name. Today, Rasiya uses photography to challenge those assumptions. Through her lens, she documents football players, flood survivors, sanitation workers, grieving families , and the everyday lives of women in her neighbourhood. Each image becomes an act of reclaiming a story that others have long told on behalf of her community. Rather than chasing dramatic moments, documentary photographers often find the most powerful stories in ordinary routines that reveal resilience, dignity and everyday life. “People here are not as others describe. They are not criminals, and this place is not dirty,” she says, as she recalls her photography journey. Rasiya is one among several young photographers mentored by Chennai-based documentary photographer M Palanikumar through Vyasai Thozhargal, a grassroots collective in Vyasarpadi that works with children and first-generation learners. Over the past few years, the initiative has evolved beyond education support into something more ambitious: helping young people discover the power of visual storytelling and use it to represent their own realities. In a neighbourhood often reduced to headlines and stereotypes, cameras have become tools of confidence, creativity, and social change. A locality that refuses to be defined by stigma To understand why photography matters so deeply here, one must first understand Vyasarpadi. Vyasarpadi's community exhibition replaced gallery walls with neighbourhood streets, turning the very place often judged by outsiders into an open-air exhibition space. For decades, North Chennai neighbourhoods such as Vyasarpadi have been portrayed through a narrow lens. Popular culture frequently associates the area with crime, violence, poverty, or social unrest. Residents have repeatedly spoken about the discrimination they face simply because of their address. “Try taking a taxi to Vyasarpadi,” Palanikumar says. “Most drivers will refuse to come inside.” Yet the reality is far more complex. Behind the stereotypes are communities built on resilience, solidarity, labour, and aspiration. Families work long hours to support children's education . Women run households under difficult circumstances. Young people dream of becoming journalists, engineers, lawyers, artists, and teachers. Many of these stories rarely make it into mainstream narratives. That gap is precisely what Vyasai Thozhargal seeks to address. Documentary photography has long been used as a tool for social change, but participatory photography goes one step further by placing the camera in the hands of the community itself. Founded in 2014 by first-generation graduates from the locality, the collective began as an educational movement focused on ensuring that children from the neighbourhood remained in school. One of its most visible initiatives is Dr Ambedkar Pagutharivu Padasalai, a free tuition centre that today supports around 150 students. The organisation emerged from a simple belief: education can become a pathway to dignity and equality. Over time, however, its members realised that access to education alone was not enough. Children also needed spaces to express themselves, develop confidence, and see possibilities beyond what society expected of them. Photography became one such space. Handing over the camera Palanikumar is no stranger to using photography as a tool for social justice. Known for documenting marginalised communities and labour issues , he has long believed that those living a story are often best positioned to tell it. “If people from a particular community tell the story, the depth and emotions attached to that are even deeper,” he says. “The way they narrate their stories itself is a political statement.” With support from Vyasai Thozhargal, he began training young residents of Vyasarpadi in photography and visual storytelling. The programme was not structured like a conventional photography class. Community-led exhibitions shift the relationship between artist and audience by inviting visitors into neighbourhoods instead of isolating art inside galleries. Instead of directing students on what to shoot, he encouraged them to observe their surroundings, speak to people, and photograph what mattered to them. Participants were given access to cameras and taught technical skills, but equal importance was placed on empathy, observation, and storytelling. For many, it was the first time anyone had asked them to document their own lives. The transformation was remarkable. Over the course of more than a year, students produced thousands of photographs capturing neighbourhood celebrations, household labour, local traditions, friendships, environmental challenges, sports, and family life. What emerged was not merely a collection of images but an archive of lived experiences. The stories outsiders never see One of the most powerful examples came from Rasiya. Following the death of football player Priya, whose passing sparked widespread outrage across Tamil Nadu, Rasiya felt compelled to document the young athlete's story. “Priya was a stranger to me,” she says. “Yet I couldn't accept that her passing was reduced to a mere news headline.” Research consistently shows that when communities create their own visual archives, they challenge stereotypes far more effectively than narratives produced by outsiders. Through photographs and conversations with family members, she created a visual narrative that restored humanity to a story many had encountered only through breaking news updates. Other participants focused on equally intimate subjects. There were images of single mothers working tirelessly to support their families. Photographs of sanitation workers taking a brief tea break after long shifts. Portraits of elderly temple workers carrying out decades of service despite financial hardship. Some students documented flooding and climate impacts in North Chennai. Others explored gender, sports, friendship, and childhood. What connected all the projects was authenticity. Rather than searching for dramatic scenes, the photographers turned their attention to ordinary moments that revealed extraordinary resilience. “The students' outlook on life, spaces, and the people they engage with is vastly different from external projections,” Palanikumar observed. Their work challenged the tendency to view marginalised communities only through the lens of suffering. Instead, the photographs showed complexity: joy alongside hardship, aspiration alongside struggle, dignity alongside deprivation. When confidence begins to grow The impact of the initiative extends well beyond photography. For many participants, the experience has altered how they see themselves. Dr Ambedkar Pagutharivu Padasalai, run by Vyasai Thozhargal, now supports around 150 children with free educational assistance alongside creative learning opportunities. Young people who once hesitated to speak in public now discuss their work with visitors and journalists. Students who had never considered creative careers are exploring opportunities in journalism, media, and visual communication. Nandhini, one of the participants, is pursuing journalism. Others have spoken about wanting to continue documenting social issues affecting their communities. Photography has also created new forms of representation. Historically, communities such as Vyasarpadi have often been photographed by outsiders. The resulting images, while sometimes well intentioned, can still reinforce unequal power dynamics. Here, the photographers belong to the neighbourhood. They know the people they photograph. They understand the context behind every image. As Palanikumar noted, the students often notice details that outsiders might overlook. Their perspective is not observational. It is lived. An exhibition on the streets Perhaps the most symbolic expression of the initiative came through the exhibition Engal Therukkal Engal Kadhaigal, or Our Streets, Our Stories. Rather than displaying photographs inside a conventional gallery, organisers transformed the streets of Vyasarpadi into an exhibition space. North Chennai has produced celebrated sportspersons, musicians and artists, yet mainstream portrayals of the region have often focused disproportionately on crime and poverty. Hundreds of photographs were displayed outside homes and along neighbourhood lanes. Visitors walked through the community while viewing stories created by its residents. The choice was deliberate. “There is a need for actual recognition of North Chennai,” Palanikumar explained. “Every photo frame was placed outside their homes so that the exhibition attendees could easily communicate with them.” The exhibition challenged not only perceptions of Vyasarpadi but also assumptions about who gets to be an artist, whose stories deserve visibility, and where art belongs. For local residents, seeing their lives represented with dignity was deeply meaningful. For visitors, it offered an opportunity to encounter a side of North Chennai rarely portrayed in mainstream narratives. More than photography At its heart, the Vyasai Thozhargal initiative is not really about cameras. It is about access to creativity, self-expression and confidence. For children growing up in communities where opportunities are often limited, these experiences can be transformative. A camera can become a bridge between observation and action. Between invisibility and recognition. Community-led photography creates historical records that future generations can inherit, preserving neighbourhood memories that rarely appear in official archives. The young photographers of Vyasarpadi are proving that stories do not need to come from outside experts or visiting journalists. Sometimes, the most powerful stories emerge when communities are trusted to tell their own. As one message from the participating students declared before their exhibition: “What you've seen, heard, known and what you've told us. This isn't Vyasarpadi. Only we can share our stories. And now, we are doing so.” In neighbourhoods long spoken about by others, that simple act of self-representation may be the most powerful change of all.
